questions.question: Describe Newton's prism experiments and explain how they showed that white light is a mixture of colours. List the colours of the visible spectrum in order.
questions.expected_answer: Newton passed a narrow beam of sunlight through a glass prism and obtained a spread of colours on the wall. He let one colour (e.g. green) through a hole and passed it through a second prism: it was bent again but stayed the same colour, so the prism does not create colours. He then recombined the full spectrum with a second, inverted prism and obtained white light again. So white light is a mixture of the colours of the spectrum. Order: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet.

questions.question: Explain, using refraction and dispersion, how a triangular prism produces a spectrum. Which colour is refracted most and why?
questions.expected_answer: Refraction: light changes direction when it passes at an angle from one transparent material into another, because its speed changes (slows in glass, bends towards the normal; speeds up leaving, bends away). In a triangular prism both refractions bend the light towards the base. Each colour travels at a slightly different speed in glass and so is refracted by a different amount: dispersion. Violet is slowed most and refracted most; red is slowed least and refracted least, so the colours fan out into a spectrum.

questions.question: Explain how a rainbow forms, where the Sun must be for you to see it, and why red is on the outside of a primary rainbow. How does a secondary rainbow differ?
questions.expected_answer: Sunlight enters raindrops and is refracted (and dispersed), reflected off the inside back of the drop, and refracted again as it leaves, so the colours separate; each drop acts like a small prism. Light returns roughly towards the Sun's direction, so the Sun must be behind the observer with rain in front. Red light leaves at about 42° and violet at about 40° from the point opposite the Sun, so drops at 42° send red and those at 40° send violet to the eye, putting red on the outside of the arc. A secondary rainbow, at about 51°, is formed by two internal reflections; it is fainter and its colours are reversed (red inside, violet outside).
